theory.title: Understanding Log Levels in Robot Framework
theory.content:
The Importance of Log Levels

In test automation, logging is crucial for understanding what happened during test execution. However, not all log messages are equally important. Robot Framework's log levels provide a hierarchical system for categorizing messages by severity and importance, allowing you to control what information is visible in different contexts.

#

The Five Log Levels

Robot Framework provides five log levels, ordered from most detailed to most critical:

1. TRACE - Most detailed, for tracing code execution flow 2. DEBUG - Detailed diagnostic information useful during development 3. INFO - Standard informational messages (default) 4. WARN - Warning messages for potentially problematic situations 5. ERROR - Error messages for failures and critical issues

#

Log Level Hierarchy

Log levels form a hierarchy where setting a level shows that level and all higher levels:

TRACE → Shows: TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR (everything) DEBUG → Shows: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR INFO → Shows: INFO, WARN, ERROR (default) WARN → Shows: WARN, ERROR (only warnings and errors) ERROR → Shows: ERROR (only errors)

This allows you to control log verbosity based on context: - Development: Use TRACE or DEBUG for detailed diagnostics - CI/CD: Use INFO for standard execution - Production monitoring: Use WARN or ERROR to highlight issues

Using Log Levels with the Log Keyword

The Log keyword accepts an optional second argument to specify the log level:

Log message level

#

Syntax Examples

* Test Cases * Log Level Examples # TRACE - Most detailed execution flow Log Entering validation loop TRACE # DEBUG - Diagnostic information Log Debug information DEBUG Log Variable value: ${var} DEBUG # INFO - Standard messages (default, can omit level) Log Important info INFO Log Important info # Same as INFO # WARN - Non-critical issues Log Warning message WARN Log API deprecated, use v2 WARN # ERROR - Critical problems Log Error occurred ERROR Log Authentication failed ERROR

#

Default Behavior

When no level is specified, Log uses INFO:

Log This is INFO level # Explicit Log This is also INFO # Implicit (same result)
Controlling Log Visibility

You can control which log levels appear in output using the --loglevel command-line option:

``bash # Show only WARN and ERROR robot --loglevel WARN tests/

# Show everything (TRACE and above) robot --loglevel TRACE tests/

# Default: Show INFO and above robot tests/

#
Practical Use Cases

During development (verbose logging):

bash robot --loglevel DEBUG my_test.robot
Shows all DEBUG, INFO, WARN, and ERROR messages for troubleshooting.

In CI/CD pipeline (standard logging):

bash robot --loglevel INFO tests/
Shows only important information, keeping logs readable.

For production monitoring (errors only):

bash robot --loglevel ERROR tests/ ` Highlights only critical failures.

When to Use Each Level

#

TRACE

- Purpose: Detailed execution flow tracing - Use when: Debugging complex keyword chains or library internals - Example:
Log Entering custom keyword TRACE Log Loop iteration ${i} TRACE Log Exiting custom keyword TRACE

#

DEBUG

- Purpose: Diagnostic information for developers - Use when: Inspecting variable values, API responses, intermediate calculations - Example:
Log API Response: ${response} DEBUG Log Parsed data: ${parsed} DEBUG Log Validation result: ${is_valid} DEBUG

#

INFO (Default)

- Purpose: Standard progress and status messages - Use when: Recording major test steps, milestones, successful operations - Example:
Log Starting user registration INFO Log User created successfully INFO Log Test completed INFO

#

WARN

- Purpose: Non-critical issues or unexpected situations - Use when: API deprecations, missing optional data, performance concerns - Example:
Log API endpoint deprecated, will be removed in v3.0 WARN Log Response time exceeded 2s WARN Log Optional field missing: ${field} WARN

#

ERROR

- Purpose: Critical failures and errors - Use when: Authentication failures, missing required data, assertion failures - Example:
Log Authentication failed for user ${username} ERROR Log Required configuration missing: ${config_key} ERROR Log Database connection timeout ERROR
Real-World Example
* Test Cases * User Registration with Detailed Logging Log Starting user registration test INFO # Debug: Show test data Log Test user: ${TEST_USER} DEBUG Log Test email: ${TEST_EMAIL} DEBUG # Trace: Detailed flow Log Navigating to registration page TRACE Navigate To Registration Page Log Filling registration form INFO Fill Registration Form ${TEST_USER} ${TEST_EMAIL} # Debug: Check form state ${form_valid} Is Form Valid Log Form validation result: ${form_valid} DEBUG # Warn: Non-critical issue Run Keyword If '${PROFILE_IMAGE}' == '' Log Profile image not provided, using default WARN Log Submitting registration INFO Submit Registration Form # Check for errors ${status} Get Registration Status Run Keyword If '${status}' != 'success' Log Registration failed: ${status} ERROR Log User registration completed successfully INFO

When run with different log levels:

- --loglevel INFO: Shows high-level test flow (starting, filling, submitting, completed) - --loglevel DEBUG: Also shows test data and form validation details - --loglevel TRACE: Also shows detailed navigation steps - --loglevel WARN: Only shows warning about missing profile image (and errors if any)
Log Levels in Reports

#

Console Output

- Controlled by --loglevel - Only specified level and above appear in console

#

log.html File

- Always contains all log levels regardless of --loglevel` - You can filter levels in the HTML interface - Click level buttons (TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, etc.) to toggle visibility

#

report.html File

- Shows high-level test results - Typically only shows WARN and ERROR messages - Focuses on outcomes, not detailed execution
Best Practices

#

1. Use Appropriate Levels Consistently

# Good: Levels match content importance Log Test started INFO Log Variable: ${x}=${y} DEBUG Log Deprecated API used WARN Log Connection failed ERROR

# Poor: Wrong levels for content Log Minor detail ERROR # Should be DEBUG Log Critical failure INFO # Should be ERROR

#

2. Add Context to Log Messages

# Good: Includes context Log User ${username} authentication failed ERROR Log API response time: ${time}ms (threshold: 1000ms) WARN

# Poor: Lacks context Log Failed ERROR Log Slow WARN

#

3. Use DEBUG for Variable Inspection

# Debug complex data structures ${response} API Call /users Log API Response: ${response} DEBUG Log Many ${response} # Alternative for detailed inspection

#

4. Avoid Log Spam

# Bad: Too many INFO logs clutters output FOR ${i} IN RANGE 1000 Log Processing item ${i} INFO # 1000 INFO messages! END

# Good: Use DEBUG for loop details, INFO for summary FOR ${i} IN RANGE 1000 Log Processing item ${i} DEBUG END Log Processed 1000 items INFO

Programmatic Log Level Control

You can change log levels dynamically during test execution:

* Test Cases * Dynamic Log Level Set Log Level DEBUG Log This is logged at DEBUG DEBUG # Visible Set Log Level WARN Log This is logged at INFO INFO # Not visible Log This is logged at WARN WARN # Visible Set Log Level INFO # Restore default

#

Use Case: Detailed Logging on Failure

* Test Cases * Test with Conditional Verbose Logging Set Log Level INFO # Normal level ${status} Run Keyword And Return Status Perform Operation Run Keyword If not ${status} Enable Verbose Logging # If operation failed, retry with DEBUG enabled Run Keyword Unless ${status} Perform Operation Set Log Level INFO # Restore

* Keywords * Enable Verbose Logging Set Log Level DEBUG Log Enabling verbose logging for troubleshooting WARN

Summary

Log levels are a powerful tool for controlling diagnostic information visibility:

- TRACE/DEBUG: Development and troubleshooting - INFO: Standard test execution progress - WARN: Non-critical issues requiring attention - ERROR: Critical failures

By using log levels appropriately, you create tests that are: - Easy to debug (detailed logs when needed) - Easy to read (clean logs for standard runs) - Easy to monitor (focus on errors in production)

Master log levels to make your test execution logs both comprehensive and maintainable.

theory.title: Inspecting Variables with Log Variables
theory.content:
The Need for Variable Inspection

When tests become complex—involving multiple variables, dynamic data, and keyword chains—it's often difficult to understand the current state of your test execution. What variables exist? What are their values? Have they been modified unexpectedly?

The Log Variables keyword solves this problem by providing a snapshot of all variables in the current scope, making it an essential debugging tool.

The Log Variables Keyword

Log Variables is a built-in keyword that outputs all available variables at the point of execution.

#

Syntax

Log Variables Log Variables level=INFO # Optional: specify log level

Characteristics: - No arguments required (simplest form) - Shows all variables in current scope - Includes test-level, suite-level, and global variables - Displays variable names and their values - Respects log levels (default: INFO)

#

Basic Example

* Test Cases * Variable Inspection ${name} Set Variable Robot ${version} Set Variable 7.0 ${features} Create List keywords libraries tests Log Variables

Output in log.html:

${/} = / ${:} = : ${CURDIR} = C:\tests ${EXECDIR} = C:\tests ${features} = ['keywords', 'libraries', 'tests'] ${name} = Robot ${TEMPDIR} = C:\Temp ${TEST_NAME} = Variable Inspection ${version} = 7.0 ...

All variables—user-created and automatic—are listed alphabetically.

What Variables Are Shown?

#

1. User-Created Variables

Variables you explicitly create:

${name} Set Variable Robot ${version} Set Variable 7.0 @{features} Create List keywords libraries tests &{config} Create Dictionary timeout=30 retries=3

#

2. Automatic Variables

Robot Framework creates several automatic variables:

Test execution context: - ${TEST_NAME} - Current test case name - ${TEST_STATUS} - Current test status (PASS/FAIL) - ${TEST_MESSAGE} - Failure message (if failed) - ${TEST_TAGS} - Tags applied to current test - ${TEST_DOCUMENTATION} - Test documentation string

Suite context: - ${SUITE_NAME} - Current test suite name - ${SUITE_SOURCE} - Path to suite file - ${SUITE_STATUS} - Suite execution status - ${SUITE_METADATA} - Suite metadata dictionary

Execution environment: - ${CURDIR} - Directory of current test file - ${EXECDIR} - Directory where execution started - ${TEMPDIR} - System temporary directory - ${OUTPUT_DIR} - Directory where output files are written

Platform separators: - ${/} - Path separator (e.g., / on Unix, \ on Windows) - ${:} - Path list separator (e.g., : on Unix, ; on Windows) - ${SPACE} - Single space character - ${EMPTY} - Empty string

#

3. Library Variables

Variables imported from libraries:

* Settings * Library SeleniumLibrary

* Test Cases * Test Log Variables # Shows ${BROWSER}, ${SELENIUM_TIMEOUT}, etc.

#

4. Variable File Variables

Variables loaded from external files:

* Settings * Variables config.py

* Test Cases * Test Log Variables # Shows variables from config.py

When to Use Log Variables

#

1. Debugging Unexpected Behavior

When a test fails or behaves unexpectedly:

* Test Cases * Debug Failing Test ${result} Calculate Something ${input} Log Variables # What variables exist at this point? Should Be Equal ${result} ${expected} # Fails - why?

Log Variables helps you see: - Current values of all variables - Whether variables were set correctly - If variables were overwritten unexpectedly

#

2. Inspecting Complex Data Structures

When working with lists, dictionaries, or objects:

* Test Cases * Complex Data Handling ${response} API Call /users ${parsed} Parse JSON ${response} ${users} Get Users List ${parsed} Log Variables # See structure of ${response}, ${parsed}, ${users} # ... continue processing

#

3. Understanding Keyword Return Values

When you're unsure what a keyword returns:

* Test Cases * Understand Return Value ${result} Some Custom Keyword arg1 arg2 Log Variables # See what ${result} actually contains

#

4. Verifying Variable Scope

When testing variable scope and lifetime:

* Test Cases * Test 1 ${var} Set Variable test1 Log Variables # ${var} exists

Test 2 Log Variables # ${var} does NOT exist (test-level scope)

#

5. Documenting Test State

For documentation or reporting:

* Test Cases * Test with State Logging # Initial state Log Variables level=DEBUG # ... perform operations # Final state Log Variables level=DEBUG

Alternatives and Related Keywords

#

Log Many

Log multiple specific values:

${name} Set Variable Robot ${version} Set Variable 7.0 Log Many ${name} ${version} # Logs only these two

Difference from Log Variables: - Log Many: Shows specified values - Log Variables: Shows all variables

#

Log

Log individual variables:

${name} Set Variable Robot Log Name: ${name} Log Version: ${version}

When to use each: - Log: Specific, formatted output - Log Variables: Quick inspection of everything

#

Variable Should Exist

Verify a variable exists:

Variable Should Exist ${name} Variable Should Exist ${undefined} # Fails if not defined

#

Get Variables

Programmatically access variables as a dictionary:

${all_vars} Get Variables Log ${all_vars} ${name_value} Get From Dictionary ${all_vars} \${name}

Practical Example: Debugging API Test
* Settings * Library RequestsLibrary Library Collections

* Variables * ${API_URL} https://api.example.com ${AUTH_TOKEN} secret123

* Test Cases * Debug API Response # Initial state Log Variables level=DEBUG # Make API call ${headers} Create Dictionary Authorization=Bearer ${AUTH_TOKEN} ${response} GET ${API_URL}/users headers=${headers} # Inspect response Log Variables # See ${headers}, ${response}, and more # Parse response ${status} Set Variable ${response.status_code} ${body} Set Variable ${response.json()} ${users} Get From Dictionary ${body} users # Final state Log Variables # See all parsed data # Validation Should Be Equal As Numbers ${status} 200 Length Should Be ${users} 10

What Log Variables reveals: 1. Initial: ${API_URL}, ${AUTH_TOKEN}, automatic variables 2. After API call: ${headers}, ${response} object 3. After parsing: ${status}, ${body}, ${users} list

This makes it easy to identify if: - API URL is correct - Auth token is set - Response structure is as expected - Parsing succeeded

Output Format

Log Variables produces structured output:

# Format: ${variable_name} = value @{list_variable} = ['item1', 'item2', 'item3'] &{dict_variable} = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': 'value2'}

Example output:

${CURDIR} = C:\projects\tests ${EMPTY} = ${EXECDIR} = C:\projects ${False} = False ${TEST_NAME} = Variable Inspection ${True} = True ${features} = ['keywords', 'libraries', 'tests'] ${name} = Robot ${version} = 7.0 @{features} = ['keywords', 'libraries', 'tests']

Note: Lists appear twice—once as ${var} (scalar) and once as @{var} (list).

Performance Considerations

Log Variables can produce large output in complex tests:

# Avoid in tight loops FOR ${i} IN RANGE 1000 ${var} Set Variable ${i} Log Variables # Creates 1000 large log entries - SLOW! END

# Better: Log conditionally FOR ${i} IN RANGE 1000 ${var} Set Variable ${i} Run Keyword If ${i} == 500 Log Variables # Only once END

Best Practices

#

1. Use Appropriate Log Levels

# Development: DEBUG or TRACE Log Variables level=DEBUG

# Production: Avoid or use ERROR Run Keyword If Test Failed Log Variables level=ERROR

#

2. Combine with Comments

# Checkpoint: After user creation Create User ${username} Log Variables # Verify ${username}, ${user_id} set correctly

#

3. Use Conditionally

${status} Run Keyword And Return Status Some Operation Run Keyword Unless ${status} Log Variables # Only on failure

#

4. Clean Up Before Commits

# Development: Log Variables # TODO: Remove before commit

# Production: # Remove or set to DEBUG level

Summary

Log Variables is a powerful debugging tool that: - Shows all variables in current scope - Includes user-created and automatic variables - Provides a snapshot of test state - Helps diagnose unexpected behavior - Requires no arguments for basic use

Use it liberally during development, but judiciously in production tests to avoid cluttering logs with excessive output.

Master Log Variables to dramatically speed up debugging and gain deep insight into test execution state.

Apply Log Variables as a debugging tool for complex tests

theory.title: Efficient Multi-Value Logging with Log Many
theory.content:
The Problem: Logging Multiple Values

When debugging tests, you often need to inspect several variables simultaneously to understand the test state. The traditional approach uses multiple Log statements:

* Test Cases * Traditional Approach ${user} Set Variable admin ${status} Set Variable active ${count} Set Variable 5 # Verbose: Three separate Log statements Log ${user} Log ${status} Log ${count}

This works, but: - Requires multiple lines - Creates separate log entries - Makes logs harder to read - Verbose and repetitive

The Solution: Log Many

The Log Many keyword accepts multiple arguments and logs each on a separate line in a single log entry.

#

Syntax

Log Many item1 item2 item3 ... Log Many item1 item2 level=INFO # Optional level

Characteristics: - Accepts unlimited arguments - Logs each argument on a new line - Creates single consolidated log entry - Supports log levels like Log

#

Basic Example

* Test Cases * Multiple Values ${user} Set Variable admin ${status} Set Variable active ${count} Set Variable 5 Log Many ${user} ${status} ${count}

Output in log.html:

admin active 5

All three values appear in a single log entry, making it easy to see related data together.

Comparison: Log vs. Log Many

#

Using Log (Multiple Entries)

${a} Set Variable 10 ${b} Set Variable 20 ${c} Set Variable 30 Log ${a} Log ${b} Log ${c}

log.html shows three separate entries:

15:30:01.123 INFO 10 15:30:01.124 INFO 20 15:30:01.125 INFO 30

#

Using Log Many (Single Entry)

${a} Set Variable 10 ${b} Set Variable 20 ${c} Set Variable 30 Log Many ${a} ${b} ${c}

log.html shows one consolidated entry:

15:30:01.123 INFO 10 20 30

Benefits: - Grouped logically - Single timestamp - Cleaner log file - Easier to locate related data

When to Use Log Many

#

1. Debugging Multiple Variables

Inspect related variables together:

* Test Cases * Debug API Response ${response} API Call /users ${status} Get Status Code ${response} ${body} Get Response Body ${response} ${headers} Get Response Headers ${response} # Quick inspection of all response components Log Many ${status} ${body} ${headers} level=DEBUG

#

2. Logging Test Data

Show input data at test start:

* Test Cases * User Registration Test [Arguments] ${username} ${email} ${age} # Document test inputs Log Many Username: ${username} Email: ${email} Age: ${age} # Test implementation Register User ${username} ${email} ${age}

#

3. Checkpoint Logging

Log state at key points:

* Test Cases * Multi-Step Process ${step1} Perform Step 1 ${step2} Perform Step 2 ${step3} Perform Step 3 # Checkpoint: Show all intermediate results Log Many Step 1: ${step1} Step 2: ${step2} Step 3: ${step3}

#

4. Logging List/Dictionary Contents

Display collection elements:

* Test Cases * Collection Logging @{users} Create List alice bob charlie &{config} Create Dictionary timeout=30 retries=3 # Log collection contents Log Many @{users} # Unpacks list: alice, bob, charlie Log Many &{config} # Unpacks dict: timeout, 30, retries, 3

Working with Collections

#

List Variables

Log Many with list unpacking (@{list}):

* Test Cases * Log List Items @{fruits} Create List apple banana cherry # Unpacking: Each item logged separately Log Many @{fruits} # Output: # apple # banana # cherry # Without unpacking: List logged as single item Log Many ${fruits} # Output: # ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']

#

Dictionary Variables

Log Many with dictionary unpacking (&{dict}):

* Test Cases * Log Dictionary Items &{person} Create Dictionary name=Alice age=30 city=NYC # Unpacking: Each key-value pair logged Log Many &{person} # Output: # name # Alice # age # 30 # city # NYC
Combining Text and Variables
* Test Cases * Formatted Log Many ${user} Set Variable admin ${status} Set Variable active ${count} Set Variable 5 # Add labels for clarity Log Many User: ${user} Status: ${status} Count: ${count} # Output: # User: admin # Status: active # Count: 5
Log Levels with Log Many

Log Many supports the same log levels as Log:

* Test Cases * Log Many with Levels ${var1} Set Variable value1 ${var2} Set Variable value2 # Different log levels Log Many ${var1} ${var2} level=DEBUG Log Many ${var1} ${var2} level=WARN Log Many ${var1} ${var2} level=ERROR
Practical Example: Login Test
* Settings * Library SeleniumLibrary

* Test Cases * User Login with Detailed Logging [Documentation] Test user login with comprehensive logging ${username} Set Variable testuser@example.com ${password} Set Variable Secret123! # Log test inputs Log Many Test: User Login Username: ${username} Password: [REDACTED] level=INFO # Perform login Open Browser https://app.example.com Chrome Input Text id:username ${username} Input Text id:password ${password} Click Button id:login-btn # Verify success ${page_title} Get Title ${current_url} Get Location ${user_element} Get Text id:user-display-name # Log results Log Many Page Title: ${page_title} URL: ${current_url} User: ${user_element} level=DEBUG # Assertions Should Be Equal ${page_title} Dashboard Should Contain ${current_url} /dashboard Should Be Equal ${user_element} ${username} [Teardown] Close Browser

Benefits in this example: 1. Test inputs logged together at start 2. Verification data logged together after login 3. Easy to correlate inputs with outputs 4. Cleaner log than 6+ separate Log statements

Log Many vs. Alternatives

#

vs. Log

# Log: Separate entries, verbose Log ${var1} Log ${var2} Log ${var3}

# Log Many: Single entry, concise Log Many ${var1} ${var2} ${var3}

Use Log when: - Logging single values - Need different log levels for each value - Want separate timestamps

Use Log Many when: - Logging multiple related values - Want consolidated output - Debugging multiple variables

#

vs. Log Variables

# Log Variables: Shows EVERYTHING Log Variables # Hundreds of variables including automatic ones

# Log Many: Shows ONLY what you specify Log Many ${var1} ${var2} ${var3} # Just these three

Use Log Variables when: - Need complete variable snapshot - Unsure what variables exist - Debugging complex scope issues

Use Log Many when: - Know exactly which variables to inspect - Want focused, relevant output - Avoiding log clutter

#

vs. String Concatenation with Log

# Concatenation: Hard to read, manual formatting Log User: ${user}, Status: ${status}, Count: ${count} # Output: User: admin, Status: active, Count: 5

# Log Many: Automatic formatting, each on new line Log Many User: ${user} Status: ${status} Count: ${count} # Output: # User: admin # Status: active # Count: 5

Use concatenation when: - Want single-line output - Building formatted strings

Use Log Many when: - Want multi-line output - Each value should be distinct

Best Practices

#

1. Add Descriptive Labels

# Poor: Values without context Log Many ${a} ${b} ${c} # Output: # 10 # 20 # 30 # (What are these numbers?)

# Good: Labels provide context Log Many Width: ${a} Height: ${b} Depth: ${c} # Output: # Width: 10 # Height: 20 # Depth: 30

#

2. Use Appropriate Log Levels

# Development: DEBUG for detailed inspection Log Many ${var1} ${var2} level=DEBUG

# Production: INFO for important checkpoints Log Many Test: ${test_name} Status: ${status} level=INFO

#

3. Group Related Data

# Good: Related variables together Log Many Request: ${request_id} Status: ${status} Time: ${duration}

# Poor: Unrelated variables mixed Log Many ${request_id} ${favorite_color} ${status} ${pet_name}

#

4. Avoid Logging Sensitive Data

# Bad: Logs password in plain text Log Many Username: ${username} Password: ${password}

# Good: Redacts sensitive information Log Many Username: ${username} Password: [REDACTED]

Performance Considerations

Log Many is more efficient than multiple Log calls:

# Less efficient: 100 separate log entries FOR ${i} IN RANGE 100 Log ${i} END

# More efficient: 1 log entry with 100 lines @{numbers} Create List # ... 100 items Log Many @{numbers}

But avoid excessive output:

# Bad: Logs 10,000 items Log Many @{huge_list} # Slows down log file generation

# Better: Log summary ${length} Get Length ${huge_list} Log List contains ${length} items

Summary

Log Many is a concise, efficient way to log multiple values:

- Syntax: Log Many item1 item2 item3 ... - Output: Each item on new line in single log entry - Use cases: Debugging, checkpoints, test data documentation - Benefits: Cleaner logs, grouped data, less verbose than multiple Log calls

Master Log Many to create more readable, maintainable debugging output in your Robot Framework tests.

theory.title: Understanding and Analyzing Test Failures
theory.content:
Why Tests Fail (And Why That's Good)

Test failures are not bugs—they are information. When a test fails, it's telling you something important:

- The application behaves differently than expected - Requirements changed but tests didn't - Test data or environment issues - Legitimate bugs discovered

Understanding how to analyze failures is as important as writing tests. This exercise teaches you to create informative failure messages that make debugging faster and easier.

Anatomy of a Test Failure

When an assertion keyword like Should Be Equal fails, Robot Framework generates a failure report containing:

1. Test name - Which test failed 2. Failing keyword - Which assertion failed 3. Error message - Why it failed 4. Stack trace - Where it failed (keyword call chain) 5. Timestamp - When it failed

#

Basic Failure Example

* Test Cases * Simple Assertion ${expected} Set Variable 10 ${actual} Set Variable 5 Should Be Equal ${actual} ${expected}

Default failure message:

5 != 10

This tells you what failed but not why it matters or what was being tested.

Custom Error Messages

Most assertion keywords accept a msg parameter for custom error messages:

Should Be Equal actual expected msg=Custom message here

#

Adding Context with Custom Messages

* Test Cases * Failure Analysis ${expected} Set Variable 10 ${actual} Set Variable 5 Should Be Equal ${actual} ${expected} msg=Values do not match: expected ${expected} but got ${actual}

Custom failure message:

Values do not match: expected 10 but got 5

Now the error message: - Explains what was being compared - Shows expected value - Shows actual value - Provides business context

#

Why Custom Messages Matter

Scenario: Testing user registration

Without custom message:

${count} Get User Count Should Be Equal ${count} ${1} # Fails with: 0 != 1 # (What does this mean? What failed?)

With custom message:

${count} Get User Count Should Be Equal ${count} ${1} msg=Expected 1 user after registration, but found ${count}. Registration may have failed. # Fails with: Expected 1 user after registration, but found 0. Registration may have failed. # (Clear: Registration didn't create user)

Custom messages transform cryptic failures into actionable bug reports.

Techniques for Effective Error Messages

#

1. Include Actual and Expected Values

# Poor: No values in message Should Be Equal ${result} ${expected} msg=Assertion failed

# Good: Shows both values Should Be Equal ${result} ${expected} msg=Expected ${expected} but got ${result}

#

2. Provide Business Context

# Poor: Technical details only Should Be Equal ${status_code} 200 msg=Status code mismatch

# Good: Explains business impact Should Be Equal ${status_code} 200 msg=API returned ${status_code} instead of 200. User data may not have been saved.

#

3. Suggest Next Steps

# Basic Should Contain ${page} Welcome

# With troubleshooting hints Should Contain ${page} Welcome msg=Expected 'Welcome' message not found. Check if login succeeded or user session is valid.

#

4. Reference Test Data or IDs

${user} Get User ${USER_ID} Should Not Be Empty ${user} msg=User ${USER_ID} not found in database. Check test data setup.

#

5. Include Timestamps or Execution Context

${elapsed} Get Elapsed Time Should Be True ${elapsed} < 2.0 msg=Operation took ${elapsed}s, exceeding 2s timeout at ${datetime.now()}
Common Assertion Keywords with Custom Messages

#

Should Be Equal

Should Be Equal ${actual} ${expected} msg=Custom message Should Be Equal As Numbers ${actual} ${expected} msg=Numeric comparison failed: ${actual} != ${expected} Should Be Equal As Strings ${actual} ${expected} msg=String comparison failed

#

Should Contain

Should Contain ${text} ${substring} msg=${text} does not contain expected substring '${substring}'

#

Should Be True / Should Be False

Should Be True ${condition} msg=Condition evaluated to False: ${condition} Should Be False ${condition} msg=Condition should be False but was: ${condition}

#

Should Not Be Empty

Should Not Be Empty ${list} msg=List is empty, expected at least one item

#

Length Should Be

Length Should Be ${list} ${expected} msg=List has ${len(list)} items, expected ${expected}
Real-World Example: E-Commerce Checkout
* Test Cases * Checkout Total Calculation [Documentation] Verify checkout total includes items, tax, and shipping # Test data ${item_price} Set Variable ${50.00} ${quantity} Set Variable ${2} ${tax_rate} Set Variable ${0.08} # 8% ${shipping} Set Variable ${10.00} # Expected calculation ${subtotal} Evaluate ${item_price} * ${quantity} # 100.00 ${tax} Evaluate ${subtotal} * ${tax_rate} # 8.00 ${expected} Evaluate ${subtotal} + ${tax} + ${shipping} # 118.00 # Actual from application Add To Cart product_id=123 quantity=${quantity} Proceed To Checkout ${actual} Get Order Total # Assertion with detailed failure message Should Be Equal As Numbers ${actual} ${expected} ... msg=Order total mismatch! ... Expected: $${expected} (Subtotal: $${subtotal} + Tax: $${tax} + Shipping: $${shipping}) ... Actual: $${actual} ... Check if tax calculation or shipping logic has changed.

If test fails, you see:

Order total mismatch! Expected: $118.00 (Subtotal: $100.00 + Tax: $8.00 + Shipping: $10.00) Actual: $108.00 Check if tax calculation or shipping logic has changed.

This immediately tells you: - Expected vs. actual total - Breakdown of expected components - Possible cause (tax or shipping logic)

Analyzing Failures in Robot Framework Reports

#

log.html

- Shows detailed execution flow - Displays all Log statements leading up to failure - Includes keyword arguments and return values - Shows stack trace of keyword calls

How to use: 1. Open log.html after test run 2. Navigate to failed test (marked in red) 3. Expand failing keyword 4. Review variables and messages before failure 5. Check error message for clues

#

report.html

- High-level test results summary - Lists all passed/failed tests - Shows failure messages - Links to log.html for details

How to use: 1. Open report.html for quick overview 2. Identify failed tests 3. Click test name to jump to log.html details

#

output.xml

- Machine-readable test results - Used by CI/CD systems - Contains all execution data
Intentional Test Failures for Learning

This exercise uses mustPass: false validation, meaning the test should fail. This teaches you:

1. What failure looks like - Familiarize yourself with failure reports 2. How error messages appear - See your custom message in action 3. Debugging workflow - Practice reading and analyzing failures

#

Why Intentional Failures Are Valuable

* Test Cases * Learn Failure Analysis [Documentation] Intentionally fails to demonstrate error messages ${expected} Set Variable 10 ${actual} Set Variable 5 # This assertion will fail Should Be Equal ${actual} ${expected} ... msg=Values do not match: expected ${expected} but got ${actual}

By running this test, you: - See how Robot Framework formats failure messages - Understand how custom messages enhance readability - Learn to interpret failure reports - Build confidence in debugging

Best Practices for Failure Analysis

#

1. Write Informative Messages

# Poor Should Be Equal ${x} ${y} msg=Failed

# Good Should Be Equal ${x} ${y} msg=Payment amount ${x} does not match expected ${y}. Check discount calculation.

#

2. Log Context Before Assertions

${result} API Call /users Log API Response: ${result} level=DEBUG Should Be Equal ${result.status} 200 msg=API call failed with status ${result.status}

#

3. Use Log Variables on Failure

${status} Run Keyword And Return Status Critical Operation Run Keyword Unless ${status} Log Variables # Dump all variables if failed

#

4. Provide Troubleshooting Steps

Should Contain ${page} Dashboard ... msg=Dashboard not visible. Possible causes: ... 1. Login failed (check credentials) ... 2. Session expired (check timeout settings) ... 3. Network issue (check connectivity)

#

5. Reference Documentation or Tickets

Should Be Equal ${behavior} ${expected} ... msg=Behavior changed from expected. See requirement TICKET-123 or contact developer team.
Summary

Effective failure analysis requires:

1. Custom error messages - Provide context and values 2. Detailed logging - Log state before assertions 3. Structured reports - Use log.html and report.html 4. Troubleshooting hints - Suggest next debugging steps 5. Practice - Intentionally fail tests to learn the workflow

By mastering failure analysis, you transform test failures from frustrating roadblocks into valuable debugging information that accelerates problem resolution.

Remember: A good error message can save hours of debugging time.

Write custom error messages using the msg parameter
Include actual and expected values in failure messages for clarity

Apply best practices for informative, actionable error messages

theory.title: Measuring and Monitoring Test Execution Time
theory.content:
Why Execution Time Matters

In test automation, performance is critical. Slow tests lead to:

- Longer CI/CD pipelines - Delayed feedback to developers - Reduced test coverage - Fewer tests run due to time constraints - Developer frustration - Waiting for test results - Missed deadlines - Bottlenecks in release process

Robot Framework provides built-in timing measurement for every test case and keyword, making it easy to identify performance bottlenecks and track execution efficiency.

Automatic Time Tracking

Robot Framework automatically records execution time for:

1. Test cases - Total time for entire test 2. Keywords - Time for each keyword call 3. Suite setup/teardown - Initialization/cleanup time 4. Test setup/teardown - Per-test preparation/cleanup time

#

Where to Find Timing Information

log.html: - Shows elapsed time next to every keyword - Format: keyword_name (00:00:02.345) - Helps identify slow operations

report.html: - Shows total test execution time - Statistics on suite and test duration - Pass/fail counts with timing breakdowns

Console output:

============================================================================== MyTest ============================================================================== Performance Test | PASS | 00:02:01.234 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ MyTest | PASS | 1 test, 1 passed, 0 failed ============================================================================== Output: C:\tests\output.xml Log: C:\tests\log.html Report: C:\tests\report.html

The Sleep Keyword

The Sleep keyword pauses test execution for a specified duration, useful for:

- Simulating delays - Test performance under slow conditions - Waiting for async operations - Allow background tasks to complete - Rate limiting - Avoid overwhelming APIs - Demonstration - Learning timing measurement (as in this exercise)

#

Syntax

Sleep time Sleep time reason

Parameters: - time: Duration (supports: seconds, milliseconds, minutes, hours, days) - reason: Optional message explaining why sleeping

#

Time Format Examples

# Seconds (default unit) Sleep 2 # 2 seconds Sleep 2s # 2 seconds (explicit) Sleep 2.5 # 2.5 seconds

# Milliseconds Sleep 500ms # 500 milliseconds (0.5 seconds) Sleep 0.5s # Same as above

# Minutes Sleep 1min # 1 minute (60 seconds) Sleep 1.5min # 90 seconds

# Hours Sleep 1h # 1 hour Sleep 0.5h # 30 minutes

# Days Sleep 1d # 1 day (not common in tests!)

# With reason Sleep 2s Waiting for page load Sleep 500ms API rate limit cooldown

#

Basic Example

* Test Cases * Performance Test Log Starting operation Sleep 2s Log Operation completed

log.html shows:

Log (00:00:00.001) Starting operation Sleep (00:00:02.000) 2s Log (00:00:00.001) Operation completed

Total: 00:00:02.002

You can immediately see: - Log operations are fast (1ms) - Sleep took exactly 2 seconds - Total test time: ~2 seconds

Identifying Performance Bottlenecks

#

Real-World Example: Web UI Test

* Settings * Library SeleniumLibrary

* Test Cases * User Login Performance Log Test started Open Browser https://app.example.com Chrome Wait Until Page Contains Login Input Text id:username testuser Input Text id:password secret123 Click Button id:login-btn Wait Until Page Contains Dashboard timeout=10s Close Browser Log Test completed

Hypothetical log.html timings:

Log (00:00:00.001) Test started Open Browser (00:00:03.456) Chrome startup Wait Until Page Contains (00:00:02.123) Page load Input Text (00:00:00.050) Username entry Input Text (00:00:00.045) Password entry Click Button (00:00:00.030) Login click Wait Until Page Contains (00:00:05.678) Dashboard load (SLOW!) Close Browser (00:00:00.234) Cleanup Log (00:00:00.001) Test completed

Total: 00:00:11.618

Analysis: - Browser startup: 3.5s (expected) - Initial page load: 2.1s (acceptable) - Form interactions: <100ms (fast) - Dashboard load: 5.7s (BOTTLENECK!) - Investigate why

This timing data helps you: - Focus optimization efforts on dashboard load - Identify if issue is network, server, or client-side - Set performance budgets (e.g., "dashboard must load in <3s")

Performance Testing Patterns

#

1. Measure Operation Duration

* Test Cases * API Response Time ${start} Get Time epoch ${response} API Call /users ${end} Get Time epoch ${duration} Evaluate ${end} - ${start} Log API responded in ${duration} seconds Should Be True ${duration} < 2.0 msg=API took ${duration}s, exceeding 2s SLA

#

2. Simulate Load Conditions

* Test Cases * Test Under Load FOR ${i} IN RANGE 100 ${response} API Call /health Sleep 100ms # Simulate 10 requests/second END

#

3. Compare Before/After Performance

* Test Cases * Benchmark Query Performance # Old query implementation ${start} Get Time epoch ${results} Execute Old Query SELECT * FROM users ${old_time} Evaluate ${Get Time('epoch')} - ${start} # New optimized query ${start} Get Time epoch ${results} Execute New Query SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE active=1 ${new_time} Evaluate ${Get Time('epoch')} - ${start} Log Old: ${old_time}s, New: ${new_time}s Should Be True ${new_time} < ${old_time} msg=New query is slower!

#

4. Monitor Incremental Slowdowns

* Test Cases * Page Load Performance [Tags] performance baseline Open Browser https://app.example.com Chrome ${start} Get Time epoch Go To /dashboard Wait Until Page Contains Dashboard ${load_time} Evaluate ${Get Time('epoch')} - ${start} # Fail if exceeds baseline by 50% ${threshold} Set Variable ${3.0} # 3s baseline Should Be True ${load_time} < ${threshold} ... msg=Page load ${load_time}s exceeds threshold ${threshold}s [Teardown] Close Browser
Built-In Timing Keywords

#

Get Time

Retrieves current time in various formats:

# Unix epoch (seconds since 1970-01-01) ${epoch} Get Time epoch Log Current timestamp: ${epoch}

# Human-readable ${now} Get Time Log Current time: ${now} # Format: 2025-10-02 15:30:45

# Custom format ${custom} Get Time %Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S Log Custom format: ${custom}

#

Measure Elapsed Time

${start} Get Time epoch # ... operations ... ${end} Get Time epoch ${elapsed} Evaluate ${end} - ${start} Log Elapsed: ${elapsed} seconds

#

Wait Keywords with Timeout

Most wait keywords have built-in timeout and timing:

# Fails if element not found within 5 seconds Wait Until Page Contains Element id:button timeout=5s

# Custom error message with timing context Wait Until Keyword Succeeds 5x 1s API Health Check ... msg=API health check failed after 5 attempts over 5 seconds

Timing in CI/CD Pipelines

#

Setting Time Budgets

``yaml # .gitlab-ci.yml example test-performance: script: - robot --maxtime 10min tests/performance/ rules: - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == 'merge_request' allow_failure: false ``

#

Tracking Trends

* Test Cases * Record Execution Time ${start} Get Time epoch Run Test Suite ${duration} Evaluate ${Get Time('epoch')} - ${start} # Log to metrics system (pseudo-code) Send Metric test.duration ${duration} tags=suite:performance
Best Practices

#

1. Use Sleep Sparingly in Real Tests

# Bad: Arbitrary sleep Click Button id:submit Sleep 5s # Hope 5s is enough? Page Should Contain Success

# Good: Explicit wait with timeout Click Button id:submit Wait Until Page Contains Success timeout=10s

#

2. Set Realistic Timeouts

# Too short: Flaky on slow networks Wait Until Element Is Visible id:modal timeout=1s

# Too long: Wastes time when element never appears Wait Until Element Is Visible id:modal timeout=5min

# Reasonable: Based on actual performance data Wait Until Element Is Visible id:modal timeout=10s

#

3. Log Performance Context

${start} Get Time epoch Perform Operation ${duration} Evaluate ${Get Time('epoch')} - ${start} Log Operation completed in ${duration}s level=INFO Run Keyword If ${duration} > 5.0 Log SLOW: Operation exceeded 5s level=WARN

#

4. Separate Performance Tests from Functional Tests

# Functional test: Verifies correctness * Test Cases * User Can Login [Tags] functional Login As User testuser secret123 Dashboard Should Be Visible

# Performance test: Verifies speed * Test Cases * Login Performance [Tags] performance ${duration} Measure Login Time testuser secret123 Should Be True ${duration} < 2.0 msg=Login took ${duration}s (threshold: 2s)

#

5. Monitor Trends Over Time

Run performance tests regularly and track: - Average execution time - 95th percentile (P95) - Maximum time - Trends over releases

Summary

Execution time measurement in Robot Framework:

- Automatic: Every test and keyword timed - Visible: Check log.html, report.html, console - Actionable: Identify bottlenecks and optimize - Built-in keywords: Sleep, Get Time, Wait Until... - Best practices: Use explicit waits, avoid arbitrary sleeps, set realistic timeouts

By monitoring execution time, you ensure tests run efficiently and applications perform within acceptable limits, creating faster feedback loops and better user experiences.

Use the Sleep keyword to simulate delays and measure timing
Identify performance bottlenecks using log.html timing data
Apply timing best practices (explicit waits vs. arbitrary sleeps)
Set performance budgets and thresholds in tests
